smes.name: Authentication
smes.owns: How every actor class proves who it is: MFA, passwordless, credential lifecycle and the strength of each path.
never_assume: That the primary authentication path is the weakest one. Account recovery usually is, and it is targeted precisely because the primary was strengthened.
That MFA is phishing-resistant. Most deployed second factors are not, and the distinction decides whether it stops the attack in scope.
That every actor class was considered. Service, machine and break-glass identities are routinely left out of an authN model that covers humans well.
That token lifetime is what the design says. Ask what the longest-lived credential anywhere in scope actually is.

must_ask.q: What is the account recovery path, and has it been threat-modelled as the likely route in?
Which second factors in scope are phishing-resistant and which are not?
What is the longest-lived credential anywhere in this scope, and what justifies it?

escalate_when: Authentication strength depends on a device posture signal another domain owns.
A customer-facing authentication decision has conduct or privacy consequences.

smes.name: Authorisation
smes.owns: Where the access decision is made and on what basis: RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC, and policy decision point placement.
never_assume: That the decision is made in one place. Ask whether two systems could reach different answers for the same subject and resource.
That enforcement points fail closed. Fail-open is common and is rarely a recorded decision.
That a role model is understood. Ask for the effective permissions of the most privileged role, not its name.
That decision logs are retained. They are the primary access evidence and are frequently treated as operational telemetry.

must_ask.q: Where is the authorisation decision made for each call site, and can two of them disagree?
Which enforcement points fail open, and who accepted that?
What does the most privileged role in scope actually grant, enumerated?

escalate_when: The PDP becomes a runtime dependency whose availability another domain must size.
Decision log volume and retention land on another domain's platform and budget.
An application's local authorisation contradicts a central policy position.
produces: authZ model with decision point per call site

smes.name: Federation & Single Sign-On
smes.owns: SAML and OIDC trust relationships, the federation inventory, and how trust is granted and revoked.
never_assume: That the federation trust inventory is complete. Trusts arrive through acquisitions, partnerships and pilots and are rarely retired.
That a trust can be revoked quickly. Ask how, by whom, and how long it takes in practice.
That claims are validated by the relying party. Many accept whatever the IdP asserts without checking audience or issuer.
That the same IdP serves every environment. Non-production frequently federates somewhere weaker.

must_ask.q: What is the complete federation trust inventory, including trusts inherited rather than created?
How is a compromised partner trust revoked, and how long does that take?
Which IdP does each environment federate to, and are any of them weaker than production's?

escalate_when: A partner trust is with a third party whose materiality the GRC domain must assess.
Federation reachability depends on network connectivity another domain owns.

smes.name: Privileged Access Management
smes.owns: Just-in-time and just-enough elevation, break-glass, session recording and the standing-privilege position.
never_assume: That standing privilege has been removed because JIT exists. Ask for the count of accounts that still hold permanent elevation.
That break-glass is exceptional. Ask for its usage rate - a rising rate means the normal path is being routed around.
That approval is independent. Shared accounts and team mailboxes let a requester approve themselves.
That session recording is reviewed. Recorded and reviewed are different controls with different value.

must_ask.q: How many accounts in scope still hold standing privilege, and what blocks their removal?
What is the break-glass usage rate, and does its use raise an alert or only a log?
Can a requester ever be their own approver through a shared identity?

escalate_when: Privileged session evidence is required by an obligation the GRC domain owns.
Vendor or support access from outside a boundary another domain declared closed.
Break-glass events need to reach a monitoring function outside this domain.
produces: JIT elevation flow with approval model
Break-glass procedure with alerting and usage rate

smes.name: Identity Governance & Administration
smes.owns: Joiner-mover-leaver, entitlement review, segregation of duties and the accuracy of who holds what.
never_assume: That leaver deprovisioning reaches everywhere. It commonly covers the IdP and misses local accounts, non-production and third-party-hosted systems.
That an entitlement review that completed was a review. Ask what proportion of entitlements were revoked - a near-zero revocation rate means rubber-stamping.
That mover is handled. Accumulated access from previous roles is the most common real over-privilege.
That segregation of duties holds across systems. It is usually enforced within one and broken across two.

must_ask.q: Which systems in scope are not covered by automated leaver deprovisioning?
What proportion of entitlements were revoked at the last review?
Which segregation-of-duties rules span two systems, and what enforces them?

escalate_when: Entitlement evidence is needed for an obligation GRC owns.
A segregation-of-duties conflict spans systems owned by different domains.

smes.name: Workload Identity & Secrets Management
smes.owns: Machine and workload identity, federation over static credentials, and the secret and certificate lifecycle.
never_assume: That workloads federate because the capability exists. Ask for the count that cannot, because that exception set becomes the highest-value target once everything else is hardened.
That the platform attests anything meaningful before issuing an identity. Ask what stops an unverified artefact obtaining a legitimate one.
That secrets in a managed store are rotated. Storage and rotation are separate controls.
That short lifetimes are safe operationally. They convert clock skew and refresh bugs into production incidents.

must_ask.q: Which workloads in scope cannot obtain a federated identity, and what compensating control covers each?
What does the platform assert about a workload before issuing it an identity?
Is the issuance path in non-production the same as production, or stubbed?

escalate_when: Attestation depends on platform provenance another domain must deliver.
Workload identity is the basis for network policy another domain enforces.
The trust anchor's protection is a physical or HSM control outside this domain.
produces: Workload identity issuance path per runtime
Non-federating exception set with compensating controls
Secret and certificate lifecycle with rotation evidence
